track.name: Accessibility & testing
track.blurb: Building interfaces everyone can use, and writing tests that catch real bugs without slowing the team down.

questions.q: What is web accessibility, and what are the WCAG POUR principles?
questions.answer:
**Accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with your site, whether they use a screen reader, keyboard only, voice control, zoom or have cognitive or motor impairments. WCAG organises its requirements under four principles, POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust. Most laws and contracts target WCAG 2.2 level AA.**

**POUR:**
- **Perceivable:** information is not locked into one sense. Text alternatives for images, captions for video, sufficient colour contrast, content that reflows at 400% zoom.
- **Operable:** everything works with a keyboard, focus is visible, no keyboard traps, enough time to complete tasks, nothing flashes more than three times a second.
- **Understandable:** clear labels and instructions, predictable navigation, helpful error messages, the page language declared.
- **Robust:** valid, semantic markup that assistive technologies can interpret, with correct names, roles and states.

**Levels:** A is the minimum, AA is the standard target (contrast 4.5:1, captions, focus visible), AAA is aspirational and rarely required site-wide.

**WCAG 2.2 (2023) added**, among others:
- Focus not obscured (sticky headers must not hide the focused element).
- Target size minimum of 24×24 CSS pixels.
- Dragging movements need a single-pointer alternative.
- Accessible authentication: no cognitive tests like transcribing codes without allowing paste or password managers.
- Consistent help and no redundant re-entry of information.

**Why it matters:** around one in six people has a disability, it is a legal requirement in many places (ADA, the European Accessibility Act from June 2025), and accessible sites are usually better for everyone: captions in noisy places, keyboard shortcuts, clearer forms.

**Practical approach:** semantic HTML first, accessible component primitives, automated checks (axe) in CI, manual keyboard and screen reader testing on key flows, and testing with disabled users when possible.
followUps: What changed in WCAG 2.2?
What is the difference between levels A, AA and AAA?
How would you start making an existing inaccessible app accessible?
mistakes: Thinking accessibility only means screen readers, ignoring keyboard, low vision, cognitive and motor needs.
Believing an automated audit score of 100 means the site is accessible; tools catch only a minority of issues.
Treating accessibility as a final QA step instead of part of design and component building.

questions.q: When should you use ARIA, and what is the first rule of ARIA?
questions.answer:
**The first rule of ARIA is: do not use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute already gives you the semantics and behaviour you need. Native elements come with keyboard support, focus and correct roles for free; ARIA only changes what assistive technology is told, it adds no behaviour.** Surveys of the top million home pages consistently find that pages with ARIA have more detected errors, because ARIA is easy to misuse. **Native vs fake button:** ```html
Save
``` **Use semantic HTML for structure:** `header`, `nav`, `main`, `footer`, headings in order, `ul`/`li`, `table` for tabular data, `label` for inputs, `a href` for navigation and `button` for actions. Screen reader users jump by headings and landmarks. **When ARIA is the right tool:** - Widgets HTML does not have: tabs, comboboxes, tree views, menus (follow the ARIA Authoring Practices patterns). - Communicating state: `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-current="page"`, `aria-invalid`. - Relationships: `aria-controls`, `aria-describedby` for hint or error text. - Live updates: `aria-live="polite"` or `role="status"` for toasts and async results. - Naming icon-only controls: `aria-label="Close"`. **Naming rules:** - `aria-labelledby` points to visible text elsewhere, `aria-label` provides a string, `aria-describedby` adds secondary description. - The visible label should be contained in the accessible name so voice users can say "click Save". **Remember:** "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA". A wrong role or a stale `aria-expanded` actively misleads users.
followUps: What is the difference between aria-label, aria-labelledby and aria-describedby?
Why is a div with an onClick not equivalent to a button?
What is an accessible name and how is it computed?
mistakes: Adding role="button" to a div and forgetting keyboard support and focusability.
Sprinkling aria-label everywhere, overriding visible text and confusing voice control users.
Using aria-hidden="true" on focusable elements, creating invisible focus stops.

questions.q: How do you make a custom modal dialog or dropdown menu accessible?
questions.answer:
**For a modal: move focus into it on open, keep focus trapped inside, close on Escape, make the background inert, give it a role and accessible name, and return focus to the trigger on close. For a dropdown: a real button trigger with `aria-expanded`, arrow-key navigation inside, Escape to close and focus back to the trigger. Today the native `dialog` element handles most of the modal work for you.** **Modal with the native dialog element:** ```html

Delete project?

This cannot be undone.

 ``` ```ts openBtn.addEventListener("click", () => dialog.showModal()); ``` `showModal()` makes the rest of the page inert, traps focus, closes on Escape, renders in the top layer and, in current browsers, restores focus to the opener when closed. **If building it yourself:** `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, a label, set `inert` on the rest of the page, focus the first meaningful element, handle Escape, restore focus to the trigger, and lock background scroll. **Disclosure dropdown / menu button:** - Trigger is a `button` with `aria-expanded="false|true"` and `aria-controls` pointing to the panel. - For an actions menu (`role="menu"` with `menuitem`s): Down arrow opens and focuses the first item, arrows move, Home/End jump, typing a letter jumps to a match, Escape closes and returns focus. - For simple navigation links, a disclosure with plain links is better than ARIA menu semantics. - Close when focus leaves or on outside click. **Selecting a value:** use a native `select` when possible, or follow the combobox/listbox pattern with `aria-activedescendant` and a live region for result counts. **Practical advice:** use a tested headless library (Radix UI, React Aria, Headless UI) instead of rebuilding these patterns, then verify with keyboard and a screen reader.
followUps: What does the inert attribute do?
What is the difference between a menu and a listbox or combobox pattern?
How do you announce changes inside a dropdown that filters as you type?
mistakes: Not moving focus into the modal on open or not returning it to the trigger on close.
Letting Tab escape behind the modal into the page content.
Forgetting aria-expanded on the trigger, or never updating it.

questions.q: How do you ensure a web app is fully usable with the keyboard?
questions.answer:
**Every interactive element must be reachable with Tab, operable with Enter/Space or arrow keys as expected, have a clearly visible focus indicator, and follow a logical order matching the visual layout. Use native interactive elements and manage focus deliberately when content changes.**

**Basics:**
- Native `a href`, `button`, `input`, `select` are focusable and operable automatically.
- Tab order follows DOM order, so keep the DOM order consistent with visual order (beware CSS `order` and absolute positioning).
- `tabindex="0"` makes a custom widget focusable in order; `tabindex="-1"` makes something focusable by script only. Avoid positive values; they create a confusing global order.

**Visible focus:**

```css
:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--ring);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
```

`:focus-visible` shows the ring for keyboard users without flashing it on mouse clicks. WCAG 2.2 also requires the focused element not be hidden behind sticky headers or cookie banners (`scroll-padding-top` helps).

**Composite widgets** (tabs, toolbars, grids, radio groups) use a roving tabindex: only one item is in the tab order, arrow keys move between items. Tab moves to the next widget rather than through every item.

**Focus management:**
- **Skip link** as the first focusable element: "Skip to main content".
- **Route changes in SPAs:** move focus to the new page's `h1` or main region and update the title, otherwise screen reader users do not know the page changed.
- **Removing content:** if the focused element is deleted (closing a toast, deleting a row), move focus somewhere sensible instead of letting it fall to `body`.
- **No keyboard traps** except intentional, escapable ones like modals.

**Testing:** unplug the mouse and complete key flows (sign in, search, checkout) using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, arrows and Escape. Watch whether you always know where focus is.
followUps: Why should you avoid positive tabindex values?
What is a roving tabindex?
How do you manage focus after a client-side route change?
mistakes: Removing focus outlines with outline: none and providing no replacement.
Using positive tabindex values to "fix" the tab order instead of fixing the DOM order.
Making interactive elements out of divs or spans that are not focusable.

questions.q: What are the colour contrast requirements, and why shouldn't information rely on colour alone?
questions.answer:
**WCAG AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (about 24px, or 18.66px bold), and 3:1 for UI components, focus indicators and meaningful graphics. Colour can reinforce meaning but must never be the only way information is conveyed, because about 1 in 12 men has some colour vision deficiency and many people use screens in bright sunlight.** **Contrast ratio:** computed from the relative luminance of the two colours, from 1:1 (same colour) to 21:1 (black on white). `#767676` on white is about 4.5:1, which is roughly the lightest grey allowed for body text. **What it applies to:** - Body text, links, button labels, placeholder text (if it conveys information). - Input borders and icons that identify controls (3:1 non-text contrast). - Focus rings against the adjacent background. - Exempt: disabled controls, logos, pure decoration. **Not relying on colour alone:** ```html

⚠ Enter an email like name@example.com

``` Other examples: - Links inside paragraphs need an underline (or 3:1 contrast with surrounding text plus another cue on hover/focus). - Charts use patterns, direct labels or shapes, not just colour-coded legends. - Status badges include a word ("Failed") not just a red dot. **In practice:** - Define colour tokens that already pass in both light and dark themes, so components cannot fail by accident. - Check every state: hover, focus, selected, disabled, and text on images or gradients. - Tools: DevTools colour picker shows the ratio, axe flags failures, and emulating vision deficiencies in DevTools Rendering panel. **Future note:** APCA is a newer perceptual contrast method proposed for WCAG 3, but WCAG 2.2's ratio is what you are measured against today.
followUps: How is contrast ratio calculated?
What about contrast for placeholder text and disabled controls?
How do you handle contrast in dark mode?
mistakes: Using light grey placeholder text as the only label for an input.
Showing form errors or chart series by colour alone, with no text, icon or pattern.
Checking contrast only on the default state, not hover, focus and dark mode.

questions.q: How do you build accessible forms and error messages?
questions.answer:
**Every input needs a visible, programmatically associated label; hints and errors are linked with `aria-describedby`; invalid fields are marked with `aria-invalid`; and on a failed submit you move focus to an error summary or the first invalid field so everyone knows what went wrong and how to fix it.** **Labels:** ```html

We'll send the offer letter here.

Enter an email address like name@company.com

``` - Clicking the label focuses the input, which also enlarges the hit area. - Placeholders vanish on typing, often fail contrast and are not reliably announced, so they are not labels. - Group related controls (radio buttons, an address) with `fieldset` and `legend`. - Mark required fields in text ("required"), not just with a red asterisk. **Input help:** - Correct `type` (`email`, `tel`, `number` only for real numbers) for the right mobile keyboard. - `autocomplete` tokens (`email`, `current-password`, `one-time-code`) help everyone and are a WCAG requirement for personal data fields. - Do not block paste in password or code fields. **Errors:** - Say what is wrong and how to fix it: "Enter a date in the future", not "Invalid input". - Validate on submit, and then on change for fields already marked invalid; avoid shouting errors while the user is still typing. - On submit failure, show an error summary at the top with links to each field and move focus to it, or focus the first invalid field. - Put the error text next to the field and keep it visible, not only in a temporary toast. - For async results ("Saved"), use a polite live region (`role="status"`). **Server too:** client validation is a convenience. Validate again on the server (zod) and render server errors with the same accessible pattern.
followUps: Why isn't placeholder text a substitute for a label?
Should you validate on blur, on input or on submit?
How do you group related radio buttons accessibly?
mistakes: Using placeholders instead of visible labels.
Showing errors only in colour or only in a toast that disappears.
Not moving focus or announcing errors on submit, so screen reader users do not know it failed.

questions.q: Explain the testing pyramid and the testing trophy. How do you decide between unit, integration and end-to-end tests?
questions.answer:
**Both describe how to balance tests by cost and confidence. The pyramid says: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests. The testing trophy (Kent C. Dodds) adds static analysis at the base and puts most effort into integration tests, because they give the most confidence per unit of effort in modern UI apps.**

**The layers:**
- **Static:** TypeScript, ESLint. Catches typos and type errors for free.
- **Unit:** one function or module in isolation. Milliseconds, precise failures. Ideal for pure business logic: date maths, pricing, parsers, validators.
- **Integration:** several units working together: a component with its hooks and a mocked network, an API route against a real test database. Catches wiring bugs.
- **End-to-end:** a real browser against a running app (Playwright). Highest confidence, slowest, most brittle. Reserve for critical journeys: sign in, checkout, the main daily flow.

**Choosing:**
- Pure logic with many edge cases → unit tests, table-driven.
- A screen or feature → integration test from the user's view.
- Revenue- or trust-critical path → one e2e test of the happy path plus key failure.

```ts
// Unit: pure domain function, many cases cheaply
it.each([
  ["2026-10-03", "2026-10-04", 1],
  ["2026-10-04", "2026-10-04", 0],
])("daysBetween(%s, %s) = %i", (a, b, n) => expect(daysBetween(a, b)).toBe(n));
```

**Guiding principle:** "The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you." Test behaviour, not implementation, so refactors do not break tests needlessly.

**Starting from zero:** add one e2e smoke test of the most important flow, then unit tests around the riskiest logic, then integration tests as you touch features. Make CI run them on every PR.

**Architecture helps:** keeping business logic in pure functions (separate from I/O) makes the cheap unit layer cover most of the rules.
followUps: What would you test first in a codebase with no tests?
Where do static analysis and type checking fit?
How do you keep the e2e suite fast?
mistakes: Writing only unit tests of implementation details that pass while the integrated feature is broken.
Putting most coverage into slow e2e tests that become flaky and are ignored.
Treating the shapes as rules instead of a cost/confidence trade-off.

questions.q: Your end-to-end tests are flaky. How do you diagnose and fix them?
questions.answer:
**Treat flakiness as a bug: reproduce it, find the cause with traces, then fix the root cause, which is usually waiting for the wrong thing, shared test data, or a genuine race in the app. Use web-first assertions and auto-waiting locators instead of sleeps, isolate data per test, and control external dependencies.**

**Common causes:**
- **Timing:** clicking before the element is ready, asserting before data loads, animations.
- **Shared state:** tests reuse the same user or record, run in parallel or depend on order.
- **External dependencies:** real third-party APIs, emails, clocks, time zones.
- **Brittle selectors:** CSS classes or nth-child that change.
- **Real app races:** double submits, unhandled loading states. These are product bugs.

**Fixes with Playwright:**

```ts
// Bad: arbitrary sleep and brittle selector
await page.waitForTimeout(2000);
await page.click(".btn-primary:nth-child(2)");

// Good: auto-waiting locator + web-first assertion
await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" }).click();
await expect(page.getByRole("status")).toHaveText("Saved");
```

- Locator actions auto-wait until the element is attached, visible, stable, enabled and receives events.
- `expect(locator).toHaveText()` retries until the condition holds or times out; a plain `expect(await locator.textContent())` does not.
- Wait for meaningful signals: a response (`page.waitForResponse`), a URL, or visible UI state.

**Isolation:**
- Each test creates its own data via API or seeding, with unique IDs; reset or use a disposable database per worker.
- Reuse authentication with `storageState` instead of logging in through the UI each time.
- Mock unstable third parties with `page.route`, freeze time with `page.clock`.

**Diagnosing:**
- Enable traces on first retry (`trace: "on-first-retry"`) and inspect the timeline, DOM snapshots and network.
- Run the suspect test many times (`--repeat-each=50`) and with more workers to reproduce.
- Track flaky rates in CI; quarantine a flaky test with an owner and deadline instead of letting it erode trust.

**Retries:** one retry in CI is a reasonable safety net, but report tests that pass only on retry as flaky and fix them.
followUps: How does Playwright's auto-waiting work?
Should you allow retries in CI?
How do you handle test data and isolation for parallel e2e runs?
mistakes: Adding fixed sleeps (waitForTimeout) instead of waiting for a condition.
Turning on retries and calling it fixed, hiding real race conditions in the app.
Sharing state between tests, so they pass alone but fail in parallel or in a different order.

questions.q: Is code coverage a good metric? What target would you set?
questions.answer:
**Coverage tells you what code your tests did not execute, which is useful; it does not tell you whether the executed code was checked properly. Use it as a signal for gaps, not a goal. A sensible approach is high coverage on core business logic, a ratchet so overall coverage does not drop, and attention to changed lines in each PR.**

**Goodhart's law:** "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Mandating 90% leads to tests that call functions without meaningful assertions.

```ts
// 100% line coverage, zero value
it("calculates price", () => {
  calculatePrice({ qty: 3, coupon: "SAVE10" }); // no expect()
});
```

**Types of coverage:**
- **Line/statement:** was the line run.
- **Branch:** were both sides of every `if`, `??` and ternary taken. More revealing.
- **Mutation testing** (Stryker): changes the code (flip `>` to `>=`) and checks whether any test fails. Measures test quality, not just execution; expensive, so run on critical modules.

**Practical policy:**
- Pure domain logic (pricing, permissions, date rules): aim for near-full branch coverage with meaningful assertions.
- UI glue and framework boilerplate: lower, covered by integration and e2e tests.
- Generated code, config, types: exclude.
- In CI: report coverage on changed lines in the PR and prevent the total from dropping, rather than one global hard number.

**In code review:** look at the uncovered lines in the diff. An uncovered error-handling branch in payment code matters; an uncovered log statement does not.

**Better quality signals:** escaped defects, how often tests catch regressions, flakiness rate, and how confident the team feels refactoring.
followUps: What is the difference between line, branch and mutation coverage?
How would you use coverage in code review?
What parts of a codebase deserve the highest coverage?
mistakes: Treating 100% coverage as proof the code is correct.
Making coverage a hard target, which encourages assertion-free tests written only to execute lines.
Ignoring branch coverage, so untested else paths and error handling look covered.

questions.q: What is contract testing, and how does it help when several services or a frontend depend on an API?
questions.answer:
**Contract testing checks that a provider (an API) and its consumers (frontend, other services) agree on requests and responses, without running them together. Each side is tested independently against a shared contract, so a breaking change is caught in the provider's CI before deploy instead of in production or a slow shared staging environment.**

**Why not just e2e:** integrating many services in one environment is slow, flaky and finds problems late. Contract tests are fast, run per service, and point exactly at the broken interaction.

**Consumer-driven contracts (Pact):**
1. The consumer writes tests against a Pact mock provider, describing the requests it makes and the minimal response fields it relies on.
2. This produces a contract file published to a broker.
3. The provider's CI replays those requests against the real provider and verifies the responses match.
4. `can-i-deploy` checks that the version about to ship is compatible with what is deployed.

```ts
await provider
  .given("job 42 exists")
  .uponReceiving("a request for job 42")
  .withRequest({ method: "GET", path: "/jobs/42" })
  .willRespondWith({ status: 200, body: { id: like("42"), title: like("Backend engineer") } })
  .executeTest(async (mock) => {
    const job = await getJob(mock.url, "42");
    expect(job.title).toBeTruthy();
  });
```

Matchers like `like()` check types and shape, not exact values, so contracts are not brittle.

**Schema-based alternative:** an OpenAPI or GraphQL schema as the contract. Validate provider responses against the schema in tests, generate typed clients and MSW mocks from it, and run a breaking-change diff (e.g. oasdiff) in CI. Simpler, but it tells you the API matches its spec, not which consumers actually depend on which fields.

**Evolving APIs safely:**
- Additive changes are safe; removing or renaming fields is breaking.
- Expand and contract: add the new field, migrate consumers, then remove the old one once no contract uses it.
- Version only when a breaking change is unavoidable.

**Real-world fit:** most valuable with several teams owning services; a single full-stack app with shared TypeScript types gets much of the benefit from the type system plus a schema.
followUps: How does consumer-driven contract testing with Pact work?
How does contract testing differ from schema validation with OpenAPI?
How do you handle breaking changes safely?
mistakes: Relying only on full end-to-end environments to catch integration breaks, which are slow and fragile.
Thinking contract tests check business logic; they check the shape and semantics of interactions.
Letting provider teams ship changes without verifying existing consumer contracts in CI.
